usage: Sits directly in front of the adjective it boosts
Pairs naturally with formal 합니다-style endings
It is a very important issue.
Modifying an adjective inside a noun phrase (중요한)
Can boost an adverb like 빠르게, not only adjectives
examples: 이 책은 매우 어려워요.
This book is very difficult.
Basic: 매우 placed right before the adjective stem
회의 결과에 매우 실망했습니다.
I was very disappointed with the meeting result.
Everyday-formal: pairs with 합니다체 in a work setting
조사 결과 안전성이 매우 높은 것으로 나타났습니다.
The survey showed the safety level to be very high.
Real situation: 매우 in a report/news register where 진짜 would feel wrong
nuance: 매우 means 'very/highly' and signals a high degree, but it lives mostly in the written and formal-spoken register — reports, news, lectures, business email — so a Korean rarely blurts 매우 to a friend. Its nearest neighbors are 정말 and 너무: 정말 carries personal sincerity/surprise ('I really mean it'), 너무 originally meant 'excessively/too much' and now also means 'so' in casual speech, while 매우 is the cool, objective booster with no emotional color. It habitually pairs with 합니다-style endings and abstract adjectives (매우 중요하다, 매우 높다, 매우 만족하다). The English-speaker pitfall: learners reach for 매우 in chat because the textbook glossed it first, which sounds stiff and bookish — like writing 'most assuredly' to a buddy. Also, like all degree adverbs it goes BEFORE the word it modifies (매우 좋다), never after the verb the way English can append 'a lot'.

mistakes: Saying 매우 to a close friend in casual chat — it sounds textbook-stiff; use 정말 or 진짜 instead (정말 좋아 / 진짜 좋아, not 매우 좋아).
Placing it after the predicate as in '좋아요 매우' by analogy with English 'good, very much'; Korean degree adverbs must precede the adjective: 매우 좋아요.
Using 매우 with a verb of quantity to mean 'a lot' (e.g. 매우 먹었어요 for 'ate a lot'); for amount use 많이, and reserve 매우 for adjectives/states.

usage: Boosting an adjective with genuine feeling
As a one-word reaction expressing surprise
Strengthens an apology to sound earnest
examples: 오늘 정말 행복해요.
I am really happy today.
Basic: 정말 conveys 'I sincerely feel this'
그 영화 정말 슬펐어요.
That movie was really sad.
Everyday: spoken reaction to a shared experience
바쁘신데 와 주셔서 정말 감사합니다.
Thank you so very much for coming despite being busy.
Real situation: 정말 + 감사합니다 layers warmth onto a formal thank-you
nuance: 정말 comes from the Sino-Korean 正(정, correct/true)+ 말(speech) — literally 'true words' — so at its core it asserts truth and sincerity, which is why it feels heartfelt rather than merely intensifying. Contrast with 진짜 ('real thing', 眞), which is the casual street twin and can sound slightly more exclamatory or skeptical; and with 너무, which stresses sheer degree ('so/too') without the truth-claim. So 정말 좋아요 = 'I genuinely like it' while 너무 좋아요 = 'I like it SO much.' It is the safe all-register intensifier — fine with both 해요체 and 합니다체 — and stacks beautifully on emotion words (정말 고맙다, 정말 미안하다, 정말 다행이다). As a standalone 정말? / 정말요? it means 'Really?!' The English-speaker pitfall: English 'really' is a one-size-fits-all booster, so learners pour 정말 into sentences that actually want 너무 for sheer degree (정말 추워요 just affirms 'it really is cold,' while 너무 추워요 conveys 'it's unbearably cold') — match the feeling, not just the word. A second trap is reaching for the punchier 진짜 in formal thanks or apologies where 정말 is the safer, more polished choice (정말 감사합니다, not 진짜 감사합니다 to a boss). Note the spelling: it is 정말, not 정말로 unless you deliberately add the adverbial -로 for extra emphasis.

Saying 정말로 everywhere thinking it is the only correct form; bare 정말 is the normal adverb, and 정말로 is a heavier, more emphatic variant used sparingly.
Forcing English word order like '좋아요 정말'; place 정말 before the adjective or verb it intensifies: 정말 좋아요.

usage: Casual booster, very common among friends
One-word reaction of surprise or doubt
Exclamation with the plain 다 ending
examples: 이 커피 진짜 뜨거워요.
This coffee is really hot.
Basic: 진짜 before an adjective in friendly 해요체
나 진짜 깜짝 놀랐잖아.
I was seriously so startled.
Everyday 반말: 진짜 amps up a casual story
그 가게 음식이 진짜 진짜 맛있어서 또 갔어.
The food there was so so good that I went again.
Real situation: doubling 진짜 for playful emphasis in speech
nuance: 진짜 is built on the Sino-Korean 眞(진, true/genuine) + 짜 and literally names 'the real thing/genuine article,' so as a noun it means 'the real one' (가짜 = fake is its antonym) and as an adverb it became the everyday casual 'really.' Its near-twin is 정말 (正말, 'true words'): both mean 'really,' but 진짜 is more colloquial, more exclamatory, and slightly punchier, so friends and younger speakers prefer it, while 정말 sounds a touch more polished and works better in formal thanks/apologies. Compared with 너무 ('so/too'), 진짜 still leans on a truth-flavor ('I'm not kidding') rather than pure degree. It collocates with surprise and strong reactions (진짜 놀랐다, 진짜 대박, 진짜 좋다) and is frequently doubled (진짜 진짜) in speech. The English-speaker pitfall: because it sounds fun, learners drop it into formal writing, emails, or speeches where it reads as slangy — there, switch to 정말 or 매우. Also note 진짜 vs 가짜: as an adverb it is 'really,' but as a noun it is 'a real/authentic thing,' so 이거 진짜야? can mean either 'Is this for real?' or 'Is this genuine?' depending on context.

Pronouncing or writing it 진자; the word is 진짜 with the tense ㅉ, and the spelling matters for being understood.

usage: 잘 + verb describing the manner of an action
Fuses with 하다 to mean 'be good at'
잘 softens into 'not quite' when negated
I look forward to working with you.
Set greeting; literally 'please treat me well'
examples: 그 사람은 노래를 잘해요.
That person sings well.
Basic: 잘하다 = to be skilled at something
저는 운동을 잘 못해요.
I'm not good at exercising.
Everyday: 잘 못하다 = 'cannot do well / be bad at'
부장님, 앞으로 잘 부탁드리겠습니다.
Sir, I'll be in your care from now on.
Real situation: fixed humble greeting on joining a team
nuance: 잘 means 'well/skillfully/properly,' and unlike English 'well' (which trails the verb: 'sleep well'), Korean 잘 sits directly BEFORE the verb: 잘 자다, 잘 먹다, 잘 하다. Its opposite pair is 못 ('cannot/poorly'), so 잘하다 vs 못하다 is the core skill axis. Watch the spacing rule, which trips everyone up: when it means 'be good at,' it fuses into one word 잘하다 (잘해요), but when it just modifies an action it stays separate 잘 자다, 잘 듣다. A near-synonym for the 'properly' sense is 제대로 ('correctly, as it should be'); 잘 is broader and warmer while 제대로 stresses 'done right, no shortcuts.' 잘 also has idiomatic softening uses: 잘 모르겠어요 isn't 'I know well-not' but a polite 'I'm not quite sure,' and 잘 부탁드립니다 ('please look after me well') is an essential set greeting. The English-speaker pitfall: do not put 잘 before an adjective — you cannot say 잘 예뻐요 for 'pretty well'; 잘 modifies verbs/actions, while degree on adjectives uses 매우/정말/너무. Also remember the negation splits: 잘 못해요 (separate) for ability, and the position of 못 right before the verb.

Writing the skill meaning as two words (잘 해요) when you mean 'be good at'; that meaning is one word 잘하다 → 잘해요, while the manner meaning stays split (잘 듣다).
Copying English order and saying '자요 잘' for 'sleep well'; the adverb precedes the verb in Korean: 잘 자요.

usage: 더 before a verb to request a greater amount
Pairs with 조금 to soften the increase
Set phrase 더 이상 + negative = 'no longer'
examples: 이 가방이 더 비싸요.
This bag is more expensive.
Basic: 더 + adjective makes the comparison
조금 더 먹고 싶어요.
I want to eat a little more.
Everyday: 조금 더 softens 'more' politely
어제보다 오늘이 훨씬 더 더워요.
Today is much hotter than yesterday.
Real situation: 보다 marks the standard, 훨씬 stacks before 더 for 'much more'
nuance: 더 is the basic comparative marker meaning 'more,' and crucially Korean has no '-er/more...than' suffix — you simply put 더 before the adjective and (optionally) mark the standard of comparison with the particle 보다: A가 B보다 더 크다 = 'A is bigger than B.' Its direct antonym is 덜 ('less'). A common booster is 훨씬 ('by far, much'), which stacks in front: 훨씬 더 좋다 = 'much better.' Watch two set phrases: 더 이상 + negative = 'no longer / not anymore' (더 이상 못 참아 = 'I can't take it anymore'), and 더 ~ -ㄹ수록 patterns for 'the more...'. The English-speaker pitfall: learners often drop 더 entirely because they expect the adjective itself to change form ('big' → 'bigger'), but 크다 never inflects for comparison — without 더 the sentence just says 'is big,' not 'is bigger.' Another trap is the 보다 direction: 보다 attaches to the thing you compare AGAINST (the 'than' item), so '내가 너보다 커' = 'I'm taller than you,' which feels backwards to English ears. Also don't confuse spoken 더 with the homophone-ish 덜; they are opposites.

Confusing 더 (more) with 덜 (less) in fast speech; they are exact opposites, so 덜 비싸요 = 'less expensive,' the reverse of 더 비싸요.

usage: I'm tired because I slept less.
덜 + verb reduces the amount of an action
It barely went down, only a little less.
examples: 오늘은 어제보다 덜 더워요.
Today is less hot than yesterday.
Basic: 덜 + adjective with 보다 for the standard
고기가 아직 덜 익었어요.
The meat isn't cooked through yet.
Everyday: 덜 익다 = 'underdone,' a key cooking phrase
주말이라 평일보다 덜 붐벼서 좋았어요.
It was nice because it was less crowded than on weekdays.
Real situation: 덜 lowers the verb 붐비다 with a 보다 comparison
nuance: 덜 means 'less / not fully / to a smaller degree,' and it is the exact mirror image of 더 ('more'): wherever you could add 더 to raise the degree, 덜 lowers it (덜 비싸다 = 'less expensive'). Beyond pure comparison it carries a very useful 'not all the way / incompletely' sense that English splits into different words: 덜 익다 = 'underdone/unripe,' 덜 마르다 = 'not fully dry,' 덜 깨다 = 'still half-asleep.' Contrast it with the flat negation 안 ('not at all') and with 별로 ('not particularly'): 덜 좋다 still means it IS somewhat good, just less so, whereas 안 좋다 means 'not good.' Like other degree adverbs it stands before the adjective or verb (덜 자다, 덜 짜다). The English-speaker pitfall: learners try to translate 'less' with 적게 ('in small quantity') for everything, but 적게 is about countable/measurable amount of an action (소금을 적게 넣다 = 'add little salt'), while 덜 scales the degree or completeness (덜 짜게 = 'less salty'). Also do not mix up 덜 with 더 in listening — one syllable flips the meaning entirely. Note: with a negative, 덜 안 ... is unusual; 덜 already lowers, so you rarely negate it.

usage: Modifying an adjective inside a noun phrase
the highest mountain in the world
가장 with 에서 marking the field of comparison
가장 can mark 'most/first' with adverbs too
examples: 이 산이 가장 높아요.
This mountain is the highest.
Basic: pick one out of many with 가장
저는 사계절 중에 봄을 가장 좋아해요.
Of the four seasons, I like spring the most.
Everyday: 중에 ('among') sets the group 가장 selects from
우리 회사에서 가장 신뢰받는 제품입니다.
It is the most trusted product in our company.
Real situation: 가장 in a formal/written superlative claim
nuance: 가장 marks the superlative — 'the most / -est' — singling out the top item from a group of three or more (이 중에서 가장 = 'the most among these'). It is the slightly more formal, written-leaning twin of 제일 (which comes from Sino-Korean 第一, 'number one'); the meaning is identical, but 가장 sounds a touch more refined and is preferred in writing, signage, and careful speech, while 제일 is the everyday spoken default. Both stand before the adjective (가장 크다 / 제일 크다). To name the field you compare within, Korean uses 중에(서) ('among') or 에서 ('in'): 셋 중에 가장, 세계에서 가장. The English-speaker pitfall is using a superlative for only two items: English loosely says 'the best of the two,' but Korean superlatives 가장/제일 want three-plus; for exactly two, prefer the comparative 더 ('A가 B보다 더 좋다'). A second trap is forgetting that 가장 modifies the adjective, not the noun, so 'the highest mountain' is 가장 높은 산 (가장 → 높은), never 가장 산. Also note 가장 is unrelated to the homograph 가장(假裝, 'pretense/disguise'); context and usually a following adjective disambiguate.

usage: 제일 + 좋아하다 in a relative clause
Singling out one spot from several
제일 used like a noun: 'the number one'
examples: 저는 여름을 제일 좋아해요.
I like summer the most.
Basic: 제일 + 좋아하다 for a favorite
우리 반에서 키가 제일 커요.
I'm the tallest in our class.
Everyday: 에서 sets the group 제일 selects from
뭐니 뭐니 해도 건강이 제일이지.
Say what you will, health is what matters most.
Real situation: idiomatic 제일이다 = 'is the top priority'
nuance: 제일 means 'the most / number one' and is the casual, high-frequency spoken twin of 가장. It is Sino-Korean 第一 — literally 'order-one,' i.e. 'first/foremost' — which is why besides modifying adjectives (제일 크다) it can also stand alone like a noun meaning 'the best/top': 건강이 제일이다 = 'health comes first,' 네가 제일이야 = 'you're number one.' 가장 is its near-perfect synonym for the adverb use, the difference being register only: 제일 dominates everyday conversation while 가장 feels a bit more formal/written. Both pick the top of a group of three or more, with the field marked by 중에/에서. The English-speaker pitfall: as with 가장, don't use a superlative for just two items (use 더 instead), and don't glue 제일 onto the noun — 'the cheapest restaurant' is 제일 싼 식당, with 제일 modifying 싼. A further nuance learners miss: because 제일 can be nominal (第一 = 'the first/best'), set expressions like 제일이다 and 제일가다 ('to be foremost') exist, so 그게 제일이야 = 'that's the best option,' not literally 'that is most.' Keep 제일 for talk and texts; switch to 가장 in essays, reports, and formal announcements.

usage: 별로 must be answered by a negative later
별로 + 안 + adjective softens the negation
I don't really want to go.
examples: 그 영화는 별로 재미없었어요.
That movie wasn't really fun.
Basic: 별로 leans on 재미없다 (already negative)
오늘은 별로 안 추워요.
It's not really cold today.
Everyday: 별로 + 안 softens the cold
솔직히 그 식당은 별로였어요.
Honestly, that restaurant was kind of meh.
Real situation: 별로이다 as a polite way to say 'underwhelming'
nuance: 별로 means 'not particularly / not really,' a soft, hedged negative, and its defining grammatical rule is that it MUST be completed by a negative form somewhere in the clause — 별로 안 ~, 별로 ~지 않다, or an inherently negative word like 재미없다/모르다. So 별로 좋아요 is ungrammatical; it has to be 별로 안 좋아요. It descends from Sino-Korean 別(별, 'separate/special') + 로, roughly 'in a special way,' which in the negative frame became 'not especially.' The standalone 별로예요/별로였어요 is an extremely common, face-saving way to say something was 'meh, nothing special' without being harshly critical. Contrast it with 전혀 ('not at all'), which is total denial, versus 별로 which is partial/mild ('not so much'); and with 그다지, a more formal/literary synonym of 별로 that follows the same negative-required rule. The big English-speaker pitfall is positive use: learners say 별로 좋아요 thinking 'pretty good,' but 별로 only points downward and needs a negative — 'pretty good' would be 꽤 좋아요 or 제법 좋아요. Also, because 별로 implies a polite letdown, dropping it as a one-word reply (별로...) signals you're unimpressed, so use it carefully about someone's cooking or gift.

usage: 거의 before a verb marking near-completion
examples: 숙제를 거의 다 했어요.
I've almost finished the homework.
Basic: 거의 다 = 'nearly all done'
저는 텔레비전을 거의 안 봐요.
I hardly ever watch TV.
Everyday: 거의 + 안 = 'almost never'
공사가 거의 마무리되어 다음 주에 문을 엽니다.
Construction is nearly wrapped up, so it opens next week.
Real situation: 거의 with a verb in an announcement register
nuance: 거의 means 'almost / nearly / practically,' marking that something falls just short of 100% (거의 다 = 'almost all'). Its standout feature for learners is the flip with negatives: 거의 + 안/없다 doesn't mean 'almost not' but renders English 'hardly / scarcely / almost never' — 거의 안 자요 = 'I barely sleep,' 거의 없어요 = 'there's hardly any.' A close synonym is 대부분 ('mostly, for the most part'), but 대부분 is more about the majority portion of a group while 거의 is about proximity to a full degree or completion; and 약 / 대략 ('approximately') are for rounding numbers, whereas 거의 says 'not quite reaching.' It collocates heavily with 다 (거의 다 됐어요), with completion verbs (거의 끝나다, 거의 도착하다), and with frequency words (거의 매일/매번). The English-speaker pitfall: don't use 거의 for an exact figure — 'almost exactly 3 o'clock' isn't 거의 세 시 정각; for 'about/approximately' a number, use 약/대략 or '거의 ~ 가까이.' Another trap is forgetting that 거의 안 = 'hardly,' so beginners read 거의 안 봐요 as 'almost watch' when it means 'barely watch.' Place 거의 before the verb, adverb, or quantity it scopes (거의 한 시간, 거의 다 왔다).

usage: I had no idea at all.
examples: 저는 그 사람을 전혀 몰라요.
I don't know that person at all.
Basic: 전혀 + 모르다, total denial
걱정 마, 나 전혀 안 아파.
Don't worry, I'm not hurt in the slightest.
Everyday 반말: 전혀 + 안 for full reassurance
그 소문은 전혀 사실이 아닙니다.
That rumor is not true in the slightest.
Real situation: formal flat denial in 합니다체
nuance: 전혀 means 'not at all / not in the slightest,' the strongest, most absolute negative degree adverb, and like 별로 it is grammatically bound to a negative — 전혀 안 ~, 전혀 ~지 않다, 전혀 없다, 전혀 아니다. It comes from Sino-Korean 全(전, 'whole/entire'), so the image is 'wholly (not),' i.e. zero across the board. The key contrast is intensity: 전혀 = 0% (total denial) while 별로 = 'not so much' (partial), and 그다지 sits with 별로 as a milder 'not particularly'; so 전혀 안 좋아요 = 'not good at ALL' versus 별로 안 좋아요 = 'not that good.' It collocates with 모르다, 없다, 아니다, 상관없다 and reassurances (전혀 안 아파요, 전혀 문제없어요). The classic English-speaker pitfall is using 전혀 in a positive sentence — you cannot say 전혀 좋아요 for 'totally good'; 전혀 only points to zero and needs a negative. Note that in casual modern speech some younger speakers jokingly attach 전혀 to a positive ('전혀 괜찮아 = totally fine'), but this is colloquial and best avoided by learners. Also keep it before the predicate, and don't confuse 전혀 with 전부 (全部, 'all/everything'), which is the positive 'entirely.'

usage: 아마 pairs with the -ㄹ 거예요 guess ending
아마도 is a slightly softer/heavier variant
examples: 그 사람은 아마 학생일 거예요.
That person is probably a student.
Basic: 아마 + 일 거예요 (noun guess)
내일은 아마 비가 올 것 같아요.
It'll probably rain tomorrow, I think.
Everyday: 아마 reinforced by -ㄹ 것 같다
지금 출발해도 아마 늦을 거예요.
Even if we leave now, we'll probably be late.
Real situation: 아마 framing a resigned prediction
nuance: 아마 means 'probably / perhaps,' expressing the speaker's reasonable guess, and its grammar is almost inseparable: it is normally completed by a conjecture ending — most often -ㄹ/을 거예요 ('will probably'), or -ㄹ 것 같다, -겠-, -ㄹ걸요. The bare statement 아마 비가 와요 sounds unfinished; you want 아마 비가 올 거예요. A near-synonym is 아마도, which is just a softer, slightly more deliberative version of 아마 (interchangeable; 아마도 can feel a touch more written or musing). Distinguish the certainty scale: 아마 is a fairly confident guess (~maybe 70-80%), 어쩌면/혹시 lean toward 'possibly, by any chance' (lower, more tentative), and 분명히/틀림없이 mean 'surely/definitely' (high certainty). The English-speaker pitfall is using 아마 with a flat present/past as if it were the English adverb that can float anywhere ('he's probably home'): in Korean the verb itself must carry the guessing form, so 'he's probably home' = 아마 집에 있을 거예요, not 아마 집에 있어요. Also avoid 아마 with established facts — 아마 물은 H2O일 거예요 sounds odd because you're hedging a certainty. Place 아마 near the front of the clause, and let the sentence-final ending do the conjecture work.
